headline: Mapping the AI Supply Chain, Fifteen Layers Deep
lede: An investor charted every layer of the AI supply chain — from silica mines to hyperscalers — to identify which companies are genuine bottlenecks worth owning on short AGI timelines. The exercise reveals that concentration of risk, not mere revenue exposure, is what separates the real plays.
body:
The question @_Lonis_ (Lonis Hamaili) asks is deceptively simple: if artificial general intelligence — *AGI*, the hypothetical point at which machine intelligence matches or exceeds human capability across tasks — arrives within a few years rather than a few decades, which public companies profit most, and which are merely along for the ride? To answer it, he built a 15-layer map of the AI supply chain, assigning each card a box width proportional to market share and a color scaled to *AI revenue mix* — the share of a company's total revenue that depends on AI demand. The result is less a stock-picking list than a cartography of chokepoints.

The top of the stack, raw materials, illustrates a recurring theme: breadth dilutes returns. Freeport-McMoRan supplies **copper**, MP Materials supplies *rare-earth* elements (principally neodymium and praseodymium, used in the permanent magnets inside data-center cooling fans and, increasingly, robotics motors), and Albemarle supplies *lithium* — but none of them derives more than roughly a tenth of revenue from AI. Their exposure is real but noisy, swamped by automotive, construction, and legacy industrial cycles. Hamaili's framework flags this as low AI beta: the company moves with the commodity, not with the model.

A layer down, the picture sharpens. **Silicon wafers** — the polished discs of purified silicon on which chips are etched — are dominated by two Japanese firms, Shin-Etsu Chemical (~32% share) and SUMCO (~25%). Both have been expanding capacity specifically for the ultra-flat 300-millimeter wafers required at 2-nanometer and 3-nanometer process nodes, where AI accelerators now live. Shin-Etsu invested ¥150 billion in late 2025 to add 200,000 wafers per month at its Shirakawa and Takefu sites. Still, wafer revenue as a share of either company's total remains modest — Shin-Etsu is also one of the world's largest producers of polyvinyl chloride — which suppresses the AI revenue percentage that Hamaili's color scale rewards.

The layer that scores highest on both concentration and AI revenue is substrates — specifically *ABF substrates* (*Ajinomoto Build-up Film* substrates, the multilayered organic boards that connect a processor's microscopic transistors to the pins that plug into a circuit board). **Ibiden**, a Japanese manufacturer headquartered in Gifu, commands roughly 22% of ABF substrate supply globally and an estimated 70–80% of the highest-complexity segment, where layer counts exceed twenty and dimensions exceed one hundred millimeters. Its electronics-segment operating margin expanded to roughly 19% in fiscal 2025, and customers have co-funded approximately half of its expansion capital — a sign of how desperately they need Ibiden's output. The material that makes the substrate, *ABF film*, is itself controlled almost entirely by Ajinomoto Fine-Techno, making it a gate on a gate: the cheapest monopoly in the chain constrains the most capital-intensive one above it.

The lithography layer — where ASML holds a 100% monopoly on *EUV* (*extreme ultraviolet*) machines, the only tools capable of printing the finest features on leading-edge chips — sits off the map Hamaili shared, but its logic is identical. Every GPU, every AI accelerator, every high-bandwidth memory chip passes through ASML's optics. ASML posted €32.6 billion in revenue for 2025, up 15%, with TSMC alone absorbing an estimated 40% of EUV deliveries. A Huawei prototype showed a functional EUV light source in December 2025, but production-ready competition is still years away.

Hamaili's framework distills to three variables: AI beta (what fraction of the business depends on AI demand), priced-in status (whether the market has already valued that dependence), and *idiosyncratic risk* (whether a competitor could substitute the supplier out of the chain). Companies like Ibiden score well on all three — high AI revenue concentration, not yet fully priced relative to a scenario of explosive compute buildout, and technically very hard to replace. The broader lesson is that the supply chain for intelligence is not a straight line but a lattice, with a handful of nodes so load-bearing that disrupting any one of them would stall the entire edifice. Mapping it is not investment advice — Hamaili says so himself — but it is a useful corrective to the assumption that the only way to bet on AI is to buy the company whose name appears in every headline.

concepts.definition: A hypothetical form of AI that matches or exceeds human cognitive ability across virtually all tasks, not just narrow domains like chess or image recognition. No system has achieved this; timelines range from a few years (among optimists) to never (among skeptics). The prospect of near-term AGI is the premise underlying Hamaili's entire investment framework.

The fraction of a company's revenue or earnings that is directly driven by AI-related demand, as distinct from legacy business lines. A company with high AI beta moves closely with AI infrastructure spending; one with low AI beta is exposed to AI but also to many other cycles, diluting the signal. Hamaili uses it as the primary filter for identifying pure-play supply-chain positions.

A multilayered organic circuit board that connects a chip's microscopic transistors to the package pins that plug into a motherboard. As chips have grown more complex — more cores, higher bandwidth — substrates have grown thicker, finer, and harder to manufacture. The film used to make them, ABF, is itself controlled almost entirely by a single Japanese food and chemical company, Ajinomoto Fine-Techno.

A chip-manufacturing process that uses extreme-ultraviolet light — wavelength 13.5 nanometers — to print the finest circuit features on silicon wafers. Only ASML produces EUV machines commercially, making it an involuntary monopolist at the most critical step in advanced chip fabrication. Without EUV, leading-edge AI accelerators at 3nm and below cannot be manufactured at scale.

A thin, polished disc of ultra-pure silicon on which semiconductor circuits are etched. The standard diameter for leading-edge chips is 300 millimeters. Wafer flatness — measured in fractions of a micrometer — must increase as node sizes shrink, making wafer manufacturing a precision business dominated by a small number of Japanese firms.

A group of 17 metallic elements, including neodymium and praseodymium, used in permanent magnets for electric motors, speakers, and increasingly robotics actuators. Despite the name, most are not geologically rare — they are difficult to refine and historically concentrated in China, which controls roughly 60% of global processing capacity. MP Materials operates the only producing rare-earth mine in the United States.

fact_check: The OCR data from the image appears internally consistent with known market structures. Ibiden's ~22% ABF substrate share is plausible for its total substrate market position; its share of the highest-complexity segment is considerably higher (~70–80% per analyst sources). Shin-Etsu's ~32% and SUMCO's ~25% wafer shares are consistent with public market-share data. The AI revenue percentages shown on the cards (e.g., Ibiden rev ~38%, op ~40%) appear to be Hamaili's own estimates rather than reported company figures and should be treated as approximations. ASML is not visible in the shared OCR excerpt but would appear in the lithography layer of the full chart; its monopoly status is well-documented. No materially false claims were identified, though AI revenue percentages for diversified raw-material companies (Albemarle, Freeport, MP Materials) are estimates subject to wide interpretation.
